claim: In Xenopus early ectoderm, the Prickle3/Vangl2 complex is polarized to anterior cell edges.
source: We show that in Xenopus early ectoderm, the Prickle3/Vangl2 complex was polarized to anterior cell edges and this polarity was disrupted by several Wnt antagonists.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing GFP-Pk3/Vangl2 localization patterns in figures and described in the text.

claim: The polarity of the Prickle3/Vangl2 complex in Xenopus early ectoderm is disrupted by several Wnt antagonists.
source: We show that in Xenopus early ectoderm, the Prickle3/Vangl2 complex was polarized to anterior cell edges and this polarity was disrupted by several Wnt antagonists.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of Wnt antagonists on Pk3/Vangl2 polarity.

claim: In midgastrula embryos, Wnt5a, Wnt11, and Wnt11b act across many cell diameters to orient Prickle3/Vangl2 complexes away from their sources.
source: In midgastrula embryos, Wnt5a, Wnt11, and Wnt11b, but not Wnt3a, acted across many cell diameters to orient Prickle3/Vangl2 complexes away from their sources regardless of their positions relative to the body axis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the effects of different Wnt ligands on Pk3/Vangl2 orientation.

claim: Wnt3a does not act across many cell diameters to orient Prickle3/Vangl2 complexes away from its source in midgastrula embryos.
source: In midgastrula embryos, Wnt5a, Wnt11, and Wnt11b, but not Wnt3a, acted across many cell diameters to orient Prickle3/Vangl2 complexes away from their sources regardless of their positions relative to the body axis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing lack of effect of Wnt3a on Pk3/Vangl2 orientation.

claim: Wnt5a, Wnt11, and Wnt11b orient Prickle3/Vangl2 complexes away from their sources regardless of their positions relative to the body axis.
source: In midgastrula embryos, Wnt5a, Wnt11, and Wnt11b, but not Wnt3a, acted across many cell diameters to orient Prickle3/Vangl2 complexes away from their sources regardless of their positions relative to the body axis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing effects of Wnt ligands at different positions relative to body axes.

claim: The planar polarity of endogenous Vangl2 in the neuroectoderm is redirected by an ectopic Wnt source.
source: The planar polarity of endogenous Vangl2 in the neuroectoderm was similarly redirected by an ectopic Wnt source and disrupted after depletion of Wnt11b in the presumptive posterior region of the embryo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Vangl2 reorientation in response to ectopic Wnt5a.

claim: The planar polarity of endogenous Vangl2 in the neuroectoderm is disrupted after depletion of Wnt11b in the presumptive posterior region of the embryo.
source: The planar polarity of endogenous Vangl2 in the neuroectoderm was similarly redirected by an ectopic Wnt source and disrupted after depletion of Wnt11b in the presumptive posterior region of the embryo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of Vangl2 polarity after Wnt11b morpholino injection.

claim: Core PCP proteins segregate to opposite sides of epithelial cells in Drosophila.
source: Studies in Drosophila revealed the segregation of core PCP proteins to opposite sides of epithelial cells (Goodrich and Strutt, 2011; Peng and Axelrod, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: The mutually exclusive localization of core PCP proteins has been preserved in vertebrate tissues.
source: This mutually exclusive localization has been preserved in vertebrate tissues and is thought to be essential for multiple morphogenetic processes, including gastrulation and neurulation (Gray et al., 2011; Sokol, 2015; Tada and Heisenberg, 2012; Wallingford, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in vertebrates.

claim: The mutually exclusive localization of core PCP proteins is thought to be essential for multiple morphogenetic processes, including gastrulation and neurulation.
source: This mutually exclusive localization has been preserved in vertebrate tissues and is thought to be essential for multiple morphogenetic processes, including gastrulation and neurulation (Gray et al., 2011; Sokol, 2015; Tada and Heisenberg, 2012; Wallingford, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established scientific understanding.

claim: Polarity cues causing the segregation of PCP complexes remain largely unknown.
source: Polarity cues causing the segregation of PCP complexes remain largely unknown (McNeill, 2010; Wang and Nathans, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles discussing the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Wnt proteins have been proposed as candidates for polarity cues due to their involvement in many PCP-dependent processes.
source: Wnt proteins have been proposed as candidates for these cues due to their involvement in many PCP-dependent processes (Gao et al., 2011; Mahaffey et al., 2013; Ossipova et al., 2015b; Qian et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2013; Yang and Mlodzik, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing Wnt involvement in PCP processes.

claim: Whether vertebrate Wnt ligands play a permissive or instructive role in PCP remains controversial.
source: However, whether vertebrate Wnt ligands play a permissive or instructive role in PCP remains controversial.
evidence: The claim represents the state of scientific debate in the field at the time of publication.

claim: Wnt proteins can instruct PCP in the Drosophila wing.
source: While Wnt proteins can instruct PCP in the Drosophila wing and orient myocytes in chick somites (Gros et al., 2009; Matis et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2013), Wnt11 has been argued to act permissively in convergent extension during zebrafish gastrulation (Heisenberg et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: Wnt proteins can orient myocytes in chick somites.
source: While Wnt proteins can instruct PCP in the Drosophila wing and orient myocytes in chick somites (Gros et al., 2009; Matis et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2013), Wnt11 has been argued to act permissively in convergent extension during zebrafish gastrulation (Heisenberg et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in chick.

claim: Wnt11 has been argued to act permissively in convergent extension during zebrafish gastrulation.
source: While Wnt proteins can instruct PCP in the Drosophila wing and orient myocytes in chick somites (Gros et al., 2009; Matis et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2013), Wnt11 has been argued to act permissively in convergent extension during zebrafish gastrulation (Heisenberg et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study in zebrafish.

claim: The Xenopus larval epidermis contains multiciliated cells (MCCs) that are coordinately aligned to generate a unidirectional fluid flow.
source: The Xenopus larval epidermis contains multiciliated cells (MCCs) that are coordinately aligned to generate a unidirectional fluid flow (Konig and Hausen, 1993; Werner and Mitchell, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies describing Xenopus epidermis.

claim: The alignment of multiciliated cells in Xenopus larval epidermis is controlled by PCP proteins during gastrulation and neurulation.
source: This alignment is controlled by PCP proteins during gastrulation and neurulation (Butler and Wallingford, 2015; Mitchell et al., 2009; Yasunaga et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It has been challenging to document core PCP protein polarization in the ectoderm before late neurula stages.
source: Nevertheless, it has been challenging to document core PCP protein polarization in the ectoderm before late neurula stages (Butler and Wallingford, 2015; Chien et al., 2015; Ciruna et al., 2006; Ossipova et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies that attempted to visualize early PCP.

claim: Ectodermal PCP visualized by exogenous Prickle3/Vangl2 complex in the epidermis can be instructed by Wnt ligands during gastrulation.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that ectodermal PCP visualized by exogenous Prickle3 (Pk3)/Vangl2 complex in the epidermis and endogenous Vangl2 in the neuroectoderm can be instructed by Wnt ligands during gastrulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Ectodermal PCP visualized by endogenous Vangl2 in the neuroectoderm can be instructed by Wnt ligands during gastrulation.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that ectodermal PCP visualized by exogenous Prickle3 (Pk3)/Vangl2 complex in the epidermis and endogenous Vangl2 in the neuroectoderm can be instructed by Wnt ligands during gastrulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: When GFP-Pk3 is supplied to the ectodermal tissue by RNA microinjection, it is homogeneously distributed in the cytoplasm and at the cell junctions.
source: When supplied to the ectodermal tissue by RNA microinjection, GFP-Pk3 was homogeneously distributed in the cytoplasm and at the cell junctions (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Drosophila Prickle physically associates with Van Gogh.
source: Given that Drosophila Prickle physically associates with Van Gogh (Bastock et al., 2003; Jenny et al., 2003), we suspected that the limiting factor is a Van Gogh homologue.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: When GFP-Pk3 is coexpressed with Vangl2, epidermal PCP becomes evident by the beginning of neurulation with GFP fluorescence enriched at the anterior cell boundary.
source: Indeed, when GFP-Pk3 was coexpressed with Vangl2, its binding partner (Chu et al., 2016), epidermal PCP became evident by the beginning of neurulation with GFP fluorescence enriched at the anterior cell boundary (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and cited reference.

claim: Vangl2 is a binding partner of Pk3.
source: Indeed, when GFP-Pk3 was coexpressed with Vangl2, its binding partner (Chu et al., 2016), epidermal PCP became evident by the beginning of neurulation with GFP fluorescence enriched at the anterior cell boundary (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In early gastrula ectoderm, GFP-Pk3 is visible as multiple membrane patches.
source: In early gastrula ectoderm, GFP-Pk3 was visible as multiple membrane patches (Figure 1D–D") but, at later stages, formed a single Vangl2-positive crescent- or chevron-shaped domain near the anterior cell vertex, i. e. the junction of more than two cells, with a ventral bias (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-D".

claim: At later stages, GFP-Pk3 forms a single Vangl2-positive crescent- or chevron-shaped domain near the anterior cell vertex with a ventral bias.
source: In early gastrula ectoderm, GFP-Pk3 was visible as multiple membrane patches (Figure 1D–D") but, at later stages, formed a single Vangl2-positive crescent- or chevron-shaped domain near the anterior cell vertex, i. e. the junction of more than two cells, with a ventral bias (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: The anterior localization of GFP-Pk3 was confirmed by the analysis of mosaically-expressing cell clones.
source: The anterior localization of GFP-Pk3 was confirmed by the analysis of mosaically-expressing cell clones (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: At the doses used, the exogenous PCP complexes did not cause any visible morphological defects.
source: At the doses used, the exogenous PCP complexes did not cause any visible morphological defects.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of embryo morphology in the experiments.

claim: The Pk3/Vangl2 complex is a sensor that allows direct visualization of PCP in Xenopus epidermal ectoderm by the end of gastrulation.
source: These findings establish the Pk3/Vangl2 complex as a sensor that allows direct visualization of PCP in Xenopus epidermal ectoderm by the end of gastrulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing Pk3/Vangl2 polarization.

claim: The anteroposterior PCP observed in Xenopus epidermal ectoderm is similar to the one observed in the Xenopus neural plate.
source: This anteroposterior PCP is similar to the one observed in the Xenopus neural plate (Ossipova et al., 2015b) and other vertebrate embryonic tissues (Antic et al., 2010; Borovina et al., 2010; Ciruna et al., 2006; Davey et al., 2016; Devenport and Fuchs, 2008; Hashimoto et al., 2010; Nishimura et al., 2012; Roszko et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in various vertebrate tissues.

claim: The anteroposterior PCP observed in Xenopus epidermal ectoderm is similar to the one observed in other vertebrate embryonic tissues.
source: This anteroposterior PCP is similar to the one observed in the Xenopus neural plate (Ossipova et al., 2015b) and other vertebrate embryonic tissues (Antic et al., 2010; Borovina et al., 2010; Ciruna et al., 2006; Davey et al., 2016; Devenport and Fuchs, 2008; Hashimoto et al., 2010; Nishimura et al., 2012; Roszko et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in various vertebrate tissues.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Pk3 is required for Pk3 membrane recruitment.
source: While the N terminus of Pk3 was dispensable for its polarization, the C-terminal domain was required for Pk3 membrane recruitment, in agreement with its ability to bind Vangl2 (Chu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited reference.

claim: The N terminus of Pk3 is dispensable for its polarization.
source: While the N terminus of Pk3 was dispensable for its polarization, the C-terminal domain was required for Pk3 membrane recruitment, in agreement with its ability to bind Vangl2 (Chu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Pk3 has the ability to bind Vangl2.
source: While the N terminus of Pk3 was dispensable for its polarization, the C-terminal domain was required for Pk3 membrane recruitment, in agreement with its ability to bind Vangl2 (Chu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Pk3 C-terminus (Pk3-C) is recruited to the plasma membrane but fails to polarize.
source: By contrast, Pk3 C-terminus (Pk3-C) was recruited to the plasma membrane but failed to polarize, consistent with the previous study of Drosophila Prickle (Jenny et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited reference.

claim: A Pk3 mutant lacking the LIM domains (Pk3ΔLIM) is unable to polarize despite being associated with the cell membrane.
source: A Pk3 mutant lacking the LIM domains (Pk3ΔLIM) was also unable to polarize despite being associated with the cell membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of the CAAX motif does not interfere with Pk3 polarization.
source: Of note, deletion of the CAAX motif, previously implicated in Drosophila Prickle polarization and stability (Lin and Gubb, 2009; Strutt et al., 2013), did not interfere with Pk3 polarization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and contrasts with cited references.

claim: The CAAX motif has been previously implicated in Drosophila Prickle polarization and stability.
source: Of note, deletion of the CAAX motif, previously implicated in Drosophila Prickle polarization and stability (Lin and Gubb, 2009; Strutt et al., 2013), did not interfere with Pk3 polarization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: Removal of the PET domain has a partial effect on Pk3 polarization.
source: Removal of the PET domain had a partial effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), contrary to the data obtained for Prickle2 (Butler and Wallingford, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and contrasts with cited reference.

claim: The C-terminus of Pk3 is both necessary and sufficient for Vangl2-dependent membrane recruitment of Pk3.
source: These data show that the C-terminus is both necessary and sufficient for Vangl2-dependent membrane recruitment of Pk3, which is a prerequisite for its polarization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on Pk3 deletion mutants.

claim: Vangl2-dependent membrane recruitment of Pk3 is a prerequisite for its polarization.
source: These data show that the C-terminus is both necessary and sufficient for Vangl2-dependent membrane recruitment of Pk3, which is a prerequisite for its polarization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that membrane recruitment is required for polarization.

claim: Pk3-C overexpression inhibits the incorporation of MCCs into the superficial epidermal cell layer at tailbud stages.
source: Notably, Pk3-C overexpression inhibited the incorporation of MCCs into the superficial epidermal cell layer at tailbud stages (data not shown), confirming the involvement of Pk3 in radial cell intercalation (Ossipova et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (not shown) and cited reference.

claim: Pk3 is involved in radial cell intercalation.
source: Notably, Pk3-C overexpression inhibited the incorporation of MCCs into the superficial epidermal cell layer at tailbud stages (data not shown), confirming the involvement of Pk3 in radial cell intercalation (Ossipova et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Several Wnt ligands, including Wnt3a, Wnt5a and Wnt11b, are expressed in Xenopus early embryos.
source: Since several Wnt ligands, including Wnt3a, Wnt5a and Wnt11b, are expressed in Xenopus early embryos (Hikasa and Sokol, 2013; Kiecker and Niehrs, 2001; Ku and Melton, 1993; Moon et al., 1993), we monitored GFP-Pk3/Vangl2 complex polarization in embryos, in which Wnt signaling was downregulated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Expression of the extracellular domain of Fz8 (ECD8) disrupts Pk3/Vangl2 complex polarization in 85% of injected embryos.
source: Expression of the extracellular domain of Fz8 (ECD8), a potent Wnt inhibitor (Itoh and Sokol, 1999), disrupted Pk3/Vangl2 complex polarization in 85% of injected embryos (n = 41), whereas only 40% of control embryos lacked Pk3/Vangl2 polarity (n = 29) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ECD8 is a potent Wnt inhibitor.
source: Expression of the extracellular domain of Fz8 (ECD8), a potent Wnt inhibitor (Itoh and Sokol, 1999), disrupted Pk3/Vangl2 complex polarization in 85% of injected embryos (n = 41), whereas only 40% of control embryos lacked Pk3/Vangl2 polarity (n = 29) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Only 40% of control embryos lack Pk3/Vangl2 polarity.
source: Expression of the extracellular domain of Fz8 (ECD8), a potent Wnt inhibitor (Itoh and Sokol, 1999), disrupted Pk3/Vangl2 complex polarization in 85% of injected embryos (n = 41), whereas only 40% of control embryos lacked Pk3/Vangl2 polarity (n = 29) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ECD8 inhibits the majority of Wnt proteins.
source: Since ECD8 inhibits the majority of Wnt proteins (Itoh and Sokol, 1999), we utilized more selective Wnt antagonists, DN-Wnt11 and the dominant negative ROR2 receptor Ror2-TM, both of which specifically interfere with Wnt5- and Wnt11-like signals (Bai et al., 2014; Hikasa et al., 2002; Oishi et al., 2003; Tada and Smith, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: DN-Wnt11 and Ror2-TM specifically interfere with Wnt5- and Wnt11-like signals.
source: Since ECD8 inhibits the majority of Wnt proteins (Itoh and Sokol, 1999), we utilized more selective Wnt antagonists, DN-Wnt11 and the dominant negative ROR2 receptor Ror2-TM, both of which specifically interfere with Wnt5- and Wnt11-like signals (Bai et al., 2014; Hikasa et al., 2002; Oishi et al., 2003; Tada and Smith, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The majority of cells expressing DN-Wnt11 lack GFP-Pk3 polarity in 89% of injected embryos.
source: The majority of cells expressing DN-Wnt11 and Ror2-TM lacked GFP-Pk3 polarity in 89% (n= 28) and 88% (n= 25) of injected embryos, respectively (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The majority of cells expressing Ror2-TM lack GFP-Pk3 polarity in 88% of injected embryos.
source: The majority of cells expressing DN-Wnt11 and Ror2-TM lacked GFP-Pk3 polarity in 89% (n= 28) and 88% (n= 25) of injected embryos, respectively (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The loss of polarity caused by DN-Wnt11 and Ror2-TM is unlikely caused by Pk3 and Vangl2 degradation.
source: This loss of polarity was unlikely caused by Pk3 and Vangl2 degradation, judged by immunoblotting (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Wnt5- and/or Wnt11-like proteins function to establish PCP in early ectoderm.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that Wnt5- and/or Wnt11-like proteins function to establish PCP in early ectoderm.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing effects of Wnt antagonists.

claim: Wnt5a promotes early formation of polarized GFP-Pk3/Vangl2 crescents that are oriented away from the Wnt-expressing clone in 73% of injected embryos.
source: Remarkably, Wnt5a promoted early formation of polarized GFP-Pk3/Vangl2 crescents that were oriented away from the Wnt-expressing clone in 73% of injected embryos (Figure 3D,I,J, n = 40).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,I,J.

claim: Wnt5a can induce an exogenous PCP axis in non-polarized ectoderm.
source: These data demonstrate that Wnt5a can induce an exogenous PCP axis in non-polarized ectoderm.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing Wnt5a-induced Pk3 polarization.

claim: The majority of GFP-Pk3 crescents are oriented away from the Wnt5a-expressing clone regardless of its position in the ectoderm.
source: By comparing the effects of Wnt5a at the lateral and anterior locations, we found that the majority of GFP-Pk3 crescents were oriented away from the Wnt5a-expressing clone regardless of its position in the ectoderm (Figure 3B-G,I-L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-G,I-L.

claim: The effect of Wnt5a on Pk3 orientation persists until neurula stages, leading to reversal of Pk3 orientation in 77% of embryos expressing Wnt5a.
source: Moreover, this effect of Wnt5a persisted until neurula stages, leading to reversal of Pk3 orientation in 77% of embryos expressing Wnt5a (Figure 3H,M,N, n = 30).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H,M,N.

claim: Wnt3a has little effect on GFP-Pk3 polarity.
source: Wnt3a had little effect on GFP-Pk3 polarity (Figure 4B,E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,E,F.

claim: Wnt11 and Wnt11b behave similarly to Wnt5a by orienting the Pk3/Vangl2 crescents away from the Wnt-expressing clone.
source: By contrast, Wnt11 and Wnt11b behaved similarly to Wnt5a by orienting the Pk3/Vangl2 crescents away from the Wnt-expressing clone (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: GFP-Pk3 is reoriented in 57% of examined embryos expressing Wnt5a RNA.
source: GFP-Pk3 was reoriented in 57%, 36% and 36% of the examined embryos expressing Wnt5a, Wnt11, or Wnt11b RNA, respectively (n >10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data quantifying Pk3 reorientation.

claim: GFP-Pk3 is reoriented in 36% of examined embryos expressing Wnt11 RNA.
source: GFP-Pk3 was reoriented in 57%, 36% and 36% of the examined embryos expressing Wnt5a, Wnt11, or Wnt11b RNA, respectively (n >10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data quantifying Pk3 reorientation.

claim: GFP-Pk3 is reoriented in 36% of examined embryos expressing Wnt11b RNA.
source: GFP-Pk3 was reoriented in 57%, 36% and 36% of the examined embryos expressing Wnt5a, Wnt11, or Wnt11b RNA, respectively (n >10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data quantifying Pk3 reorientation.

claim: PCP can be instructed by Wnt5a, Wnt11, and Wnt11b, but less so by Wnt3a.
source: These results suggest that PCP can be instructed by these Wnt ligands, but less so by Wnt3a that acts preferentially through the β-catenin-dependent pathway (Kikuchi et al., 2009; Semenov et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and cited references about Wnt3a signaling.

claim: Wnt3a acts preferentially through the β-catenin-dependent pathway.
source: These results suggest that PCP can be instructed by these Wnt ligands, but less so by Wnt3a that acts preferentially through the β-catenin-dependent pathway (Kikuchi et al., 2009; Semenov et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microtubules play a critical role in PCP.
source: Since microtubules play a critical role in PCP (Chien et al., 2015; Matis et al., 2014; Vladar et al., 2012), we examined the microtubule orientation at midgastrula stages by monitoring the movement of CLIP-170-GFP and EB1-GFP, two microtubule plus-end-binding proteins (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CLIP-170 and EB1 are microtubule plus-end-binding proteins.
source: Since microtubules play a critical role in PCP (Chien et al., 2015; Matis et al., 2014; Vladar et al., 2012), we examined the microtubule orientation at midgastrula stages by monitoring the movement of CLIP-170-GFP and EB1-GFP, two microtubule plus-end-binding proteins (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Control embryos show a weak alignment of CLIP170-GFP traces along the TFP clone border.
source: In a similar experimental setting (Figure 4A), control embryos showed a weak alignment of CLIP170-GFP traces along the TFP clone border (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Video 1.

claim: A slight reorientation of CLIP170-GFP traces was detected towards the border of the Wnt5a clone, yet the difference was insignificant.
source: A slight reorientation of CLIP170-GFP traces was detected towards the border of the Wnt5a clone, yet the difference was insignificant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither live imaging of EB1-GFP nor analysis of stable microtubules visualized by Ensconsin-GFP revealed a significant effect of Wnt5a on microtubule alignment.
source: In addition, neither live imaging of EB1-GFP nor analysis of stable microtubules visualized by the microtubule-binding protein Ensconsin-GFP revealed a significant effect of Wnt5a on microtubule alignment (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (not shown).

claim: Wnt signaling might regulate core PCP proteins without reorganizing microtubules in this system.
source: Thus, Wnt signaling might regulate core PCP proteins without reorganizing microtubules in this system, as opposed to the Drosophila wing (Matis et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and contrasts with cited reference.

claim: There is no detectable bias in the position of centrosomes marked by γ-tubulin staining.
source: Similarly, there was no detectable bias in the position of centrosomes marked by γ-tubulin staining (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (not shown).

claim: Core PCP proteins likely represent an early response to Wnt signaling.
source: Since core PCP proteins likely represent an early response to Wnt signaling, morphological manifestations of PCP may not be fully apparent until later developmental stages.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Morphological manifestations of PCP may not be fully apparent until later developmental stages.
source: Since core PCP proteins likely represent an early response to Wnt signaling, morphological manifestations of PCP may not be fully apparent until later developmental stages.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Vangl2 is polarized in neuroectoderm but is poorly detectable in the epidermis.
source: To demonstrate the effect of Wnts on an endogenous PCP marker, we evaluated Vangl2 that is polarized in neuroectoderm but is poorly detectable in the epidermis (Ossipova et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Vangl2 is reoriented away from a source of Wnt5a in 90% of injected embryos.
source: Compared to its anterior polarization in control neuroectodermal cells, Vangl2 was reoriented away from a source of Wnt5a (Figure 5A–D). Such effect was observed in 90% of injected embryos (n = 46), but it was only visible in cells located one to four cell diameters away from the border of the Wnt5a clone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: The reorientation of Vangl2 by Wnt5a is only visible in cells located one to four cell diameters away from the border of the Wnt5a clone.
source: Compared to its anterior polarization in control neuroectodermal cells, Vangl2 was reoriented away from a source of Wnt5a (Figure 5A–D). Such effect was observed in 90% of injected embryos (n = 46), but it was only visible in cells located one to four cell diameters away from the border of the Wnt5a clone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The anterior polarization of Vangl2 results from endogenous Wnt proteins secreted from the posterior end of the embryo.
source: This finding supports our conclusions obtained for ectopic Pk3/Vangl2 complexes and suggests that the anterior polarization of Vangl2 results from endogenous Wnt proteins secreted from the posterior end of the embryo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing Vangl2 reorientation by ectopic Wnt5a.

claim: Wnt5a and Wnt11b are non-canonical Wnt ligands expressed at the posterior region of gastrula embryos.
source: To elucidate which Wnt ligands might be responsible, we knocked down Wnt5a and Wnt11b, two non-canonical Wnt ligands expressed at the posterior region of gastrula embryos (Ku and Melton, 1993; Moon et al., 1993), using previously characterized morpholino oligonucleotides (Pandur et al., 2002; Schambony and Wedlich, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Vangl2 is accumulated at the anterior borders of cells in 87% of control embryos.
source: Whereas Vangl2 was accumulated at the anterior borders of cells in control embryos (87%, n = 24) and Wnt5a-depleted embryos (90%, n = 28), this polarity was retained only in 59% of embryos depleted of Wnt11b (n = 32) (Figure 5E,F and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Vangl2 is accumulated at the anterior borders of cells in 90% of Wnt5a-depleted embryos.
